flashcards.q: What precondition must hold for cyclic sort to apply at all?
flashcards.a: The array must contain n (or n-1) values drawn from a known, contiguous range tied to the array's own length, such as [1,n] or [0,n-1]. Without that range constraint, the technique doesn't apply.

flashcards.q: Cyclic sort has a while loop nested inside another loop -- why is the total complexity O(n), not O(n^2)?
flashcards.a: Every swap permanently places one value into its correct final home index, and a placed value is never moved again. Since there are only n values, the total number of swaps across the ENTIRE run is bounded by n, not n per outer index.

flashcards.q: What is the single most common implementation bug in cyclic sort?
flashcards.a: Advancing the index pointer i on every loop iteration regardless of whether a swap happened. i must only advance once the value currently at i is confirmed already in its home slot.

flashcards.q: In the negative-marking variant (Find All Numbers Disappeared, LC448), why must you read nums[abs(v)-1] instead of nums[v-1]?
flashcards.a: Earlier iterations may have already negated the value at that slot (marking a different value as seen). Reading v-1 directly on an already-negated v would compute an invalid negative array index.

flashcards.q: In First Missing Positive (LC41), why must you skip values outside the range [1,n] during placement instead of attempting to swap them?
flashcards.a: A value outside [1,n] has no valid home index in a length-n array and can never be 'the first missing positive' anyway (the answer is always in [1,n+1] by pigeonhole), so attempting to place it would either crash with an out-of-bounds index or corrupt an unrelated slot.

flashcards.q: For Missing Number (LC268), why is the home index for value v just 'v' instead of 'v - 1' as in the [1,n] variants?
flashcards.a: LC268's range is [0, n], a 0-indexed range, so value v's natural home is index v itself; the [1,n]-range formula (value - 1) only applies when the valid values start at 1.

flashcards.q: If a problem explicitly says the input array cannot be modified, can you still use cyclic sort or negative marking?
flashcards.a: No. Both techniques require in-place mutation. If mutation is disallowed (e.g. a stricter version of Find the Duplicate Number), fall back to Floyd's cycle detection (treating nums[i] as an implicit linked-list pointer) or binary search over the value range.

flashcards.q: How can Set Mismatch (LC645) -- find the duplicate AND the missing number -- be solved without any array mutation at all?
flashcards.a: Two equations from sums: sum(nums) - sum(1..n) = duplicate - missing, and sum(nums^2) - sum((1..n)^2) = duplicate^2 - missing^2 = (duplicate-missing)(duplicate+missing). Solve the two equations for the two unknowns, watching for overflow on the squared sum for large n.

flashcards.q: Why does Kth Missing Positive Number (LC1060) NOT use cyclic sort even though it's about missing positive numbers, if the input is already sorted?
flashcards.a: A sorted input lets you binary search directly for the index where arr[i] - (i+1) >= k (counting missing positives before each element), giving O(log n) -- strictly better than an O(n) cyclic-sort-style linear pass, so binary search is the correct tool once sortedness is given.

flashcards.q: Why does Array Nesting (LC565) look like cyclic sort but actually require a different technique?
flashcards.a: Array Nesting asks for the length of the longest cycle in the implicit functional graph next(i) = nums[i] -- a cycle-length/graph traversal problem, not a per-value home-index placement problem. Cyclic sort requires each value to have one well-defined home derived from its own value; Array Nesting cares about cycle structure, closer to the fast/slow-pointer 'array as linked list' trick.
